author: Erich Fromm

content: Psychoanalytic Review, 104(4), August 2017 © 2017 N.P.A.P. LYNN S. CHANCER SADOMASOCHISM OR THE ART OF LOVING SADOMASOCHISM OR THE ART OF LOVING: Fromm and Feminist Theory Lynn S. Chancer Although the work of Erich Fromm is not usually associated with feminist theory, his ideas overall are more consonant with contemporary notions of gender than usually recognized. This paper identifies three aspects of Fromm’s thought worth femi- nist revisiting. The first relates to Fromm’s gender-less use of sadomasochism to describe relationships based on dominance and subordination; this framework can be applied to sexist dy- namics, though not limited to this context. Second, Fromm’s vi- sion of love as presented in The Art of Loving can be seen as kindred with Simone de Beauvoir’s critique of romantic love and its flaws. Third, and relatedly, Fromm’s concerns about the need for recognition as well as autonomy are compatible with Jessica Benjamin’s notion of mutual recognition as developed in her book The Bonds of Love. All told, Frommian and femi- nist thought appear to be more connected than antagonistic. FROMM AND FEMINISM: REVISITING AN OVERLOOKED RELATIONSHIP It is hardly coincidental that, at the same time authoritarian move- ments are resurging in capitalist societies around the globe, the relevance of Erich Fromm’s work is also undergoing rediscovery. Recent conferences have been organized by sociologists in the United States and Canada on the Frankfurt School and Fromm’s ideas; a new Fromm professorship was recently created in Ber- lin; and special journal issues like the present one are appear- ing. Taken together, these events attest to renewed scholarly and social/political interest in what Scottish scholar Kieran Durkin (2014) calls the “radical humanism” of Erich Fromm. However, the salience of Fromm’s work is much less evident when it comes to countermovements that have registered passionate protests against another liberatory form of cultural change: feminism and the diverse feminisms that emerged from the 1960s on, intent on furthering human happiness through critiques of gender in-

470 LYNN S. CHANCER equalities and widening possibilities of intimate relationships and sexual freedom. Indeed, few feminist theorists cite Fromm’s work as a major inspiration, and it is striking that recent Fromm schol- arship is penned disproportionately (though not exclusively) by men. See, for counterexamples, writings by Joan Braune (2015) and Sandra Buechler (2015). But why such neglect when—as this essay strives to demonstrate—Fromm’s thought was consonant with both feminist critiques and humanist hopes of expanding personal and political fulfillment? Here I posit that, while not necessarily obvious or well-known, the work of Erich Fromm merits a second look from a feminist standpoint; more of interest can be found than a superficial glance would reveal. Nevertheless, in some respects, Fromm’s relevance for contemporary feminism is something of a “mixed bag.” While until recently Fromm has been a relatively “forgotten intellectual,” as social theorist Neil McLaughlin (2017) explains in his contribu- tion to this issue, Fromm was nonetheless ahead of his time when it came to his indictments of patriarchy and sexism, both out- side and inside the Freudian psychoanalytic establishment. Mean- ingful here is that Fromm worked closely with Karen Horney as she was developing and promoting her feminist-attuned psycho- analytic lens. By virtue of this and other political associations, Fromm was more than willing to both acknowledge and criticize Freud’s patriarchal biases. Perhaps it should not be surprising, then, that Fromm’s writings seem anticipatory of several early radical feminist ideas. On the other hand, Fromm’s usually exem- plary ability to merge the psychoanalytic and the sociological was strikingly absent from the biologically oriented essentialism that comes through in published reflections on “mother right” and “feminine nature.” Overall, this paper’s goal is to show the importance of Fromm’s contributions for overcoming the still-prevalent assumption that Freudian psychoanalytic theories are incompatible with feminist analysis and convictions in respect to the social character and origins of gender inequality. Since I discuss both the contribu- tions and pitfalls of Fromm’s work, I aim to draw on the former and point beyond the latter. To begin, I outline three interwoven advantages of Fromm’s thought which I believe are applicable and akin to much contemporary feminist theorizing. These are, first, Fromm’s nonessentialist rendering of dominance and subordi-

SADOMASOCHISM OR THE ART OF LOVING 471 nate relationships that are helpful for understanding oppressed/ oppressor dynamics operative in gendered and other social re- lationships. For Fromm, sadism and masochism are not at all biologically based, but, rather, defenses best diagnosed as aris- ing alongside emerging capitalism. Second, Fromm’s rendering of love is consistent with feminist critiques of the nuclear family going back to Simone de Beauvoir’s (1949) seminal The Second Sex and continuing into radical and queer feminist thought. Third, Fromm’s ideas offer an alternative vision of liberatory love be- cause it prefigured the more recent notion of mutual recognition, as elaborated by Jessica Benjamin (1988) in her fine work of psy- choanalytic feminism, The Bonds of Love. After exploring these affinities with feminisms, I turn to an- other side of Fromm’s thought regarding gender and sexuality, namely, Fromm’s essentialist-sounding notions of matriarchy and feminine nature as expressed elsewhere in his writings. Social constructionist as well as determinist aspects appear in the course of surveying connections between Fromm and feminisms, raising a question as to how, or if, this contradiction can be resolved to avoid jettisoning the proverbial “baby with the bathwater” when considering Fromm’s contributions in sum. FROMM AND FEMINISM: A TRIO OF KINDRED INSIGHTS Looking back on my doctoral dissertation that later became the book, Sadomasochism in Everyday Life: Dynamics of Power and Po- werlessness (Chancer, 1992), I note that Fromm’s ideas were not only consistent with but inspiring of my own intellectual evolu- tion. In Escape From Freedom, Fromm (1941) famously argued that people need to defend themselves against the loneliness and ano- mie of modern gesellschaft societies, against a need that can take the form of submitting to a more powerful being—thus, yielding to masochism—or exerting control over a relatively powerless par- ty—sadism. Interestingly, whereas Freud uses defense mechanisms to indicate responses to conflicts emanating from an individual’s childhood relationships, Fromm’s “mechanisms of escape”—sa- dism, masochism, and automaton conformity—should far more properly be dubbed social defense mechanisms, a term badly in need of a more precise definition and theoretical expansion.

472 LYNN S. CHANCER Here, though, one finds social defenses already alive in Fromm’s conceptualizations. Indeed, in Escape From Freedom, he describes social defenses quite precisely as interpersonal mechanisms to which people resort in response to social anxieties experienced in the face of lost or frighteningly unavailable human connec- tions. Thus, in that book, as in other writings, Fromm starts from deeply sociological, not only psychological, premises, revealing his orientation to be truly “psychosocial” in comprehending the multidimensionality of human experience. Noteworthy for feminist appropriation, though, is that nothing about Fromm’s characterization of sadism and masochism as psy- chosocial defense mechanisms is intrinsically gendered. Rather than weaving links of biological causality between masochism and women, which unfortunately characterizes writings on mas- ochism by Helene Deutsch (1944) with which Fromm would have been familiar, Escape From Freedom provides no indication what- soever that sadism is inherently the province of men nor mas- ochism that of women. Clearly, Fromm makes generic, species- based usage of the word “man,” but neither his analyses in Escape From Freedom nor those in The Sane Society (Fromm, 1956), which sketches an alternative to sadomasochistic societies, provides evi- dence that what is said is confined to any particular species or gender—woman, man, or person. This is certainly for the better, but also possibly for the worse, since a simultaneously gendered analysis could have further enriched his observations. Still, in Fromm’s approach, one finds concepts that appear genderless and unabashedly humanistic. Yet, while Fromm himself did not go beyond his pointedly so- cial and historical illuminations of sadomasochistic defenses by “applying” them to sexist dynamics, extensions of his analyses to gender questions are easy to make. As I contended in Sadomaso- chism in Everyday Life, patterned gender socialization in tradition- al nuclear families have tended to encourage women into relative- ly more submissive habits—indeed, as Bourdieu (1987) would say, into a relatively more subordinated gendered habitus—whereas men learn to adopt the relatively more aggressive postures of the “sadist.” One can readily draw on Fromm’s nonessential depic- tions of sadism and masochism to paint an even more complex picture. As Freud and others have postulated, both sadism and masochism can be present and transformable, depending on the

SADOMASOCHISM OR THE ART OF LOVING 473 context, within the same individual. Thus, someone enculturated into “femininity” may enact (say) relative submissiveness toward a male partner/husband who demands this, while enacting (say) sa- dism toward others in her life, like a child, whose experiences she is better able to control. In both modes—comprising what I called dominant masochism and subordinate sadism in Sadomasochism in Everyday Life (Chancer, 1992)—sadomasochistic dynamics beget connections that defend against the abject terror of aloneness/ deathliness/emptiness. On the other hand, anyone familiar with the writings of Jean Genet on this subject, or with ethnographic studies, such as the one of dominatrixes undertaken so well by sociologist Danielle Lindemann (2012), knows the clichéd but seemingly empirically well-founded stories about cases of power- ful men who enact (say) dominant sadism in their daytime busi- ness dealings while turning to (say) subordinate masochism dur- ing paid evening visits to satisfy their sexual desires for domina- tion by another. Consequently, patterns arise that are not biologically given but sociologically changeable depending on stratifications of class, race, and, of course, gender. It is a nonessentialism extremely consonant with feminist theoretical insistence on the socially con- structed and “situated” character of patterns that incline—yet do not determine—patterns of dominance and subordination, pow- er/powerlessness, in the form of masochism for her (or him) or sadism for him (or her) (Chancer, 1992, chapter 2). This analysis, as I have traced it from Fromm to feminism, also leaves open varied permutations and combinations of sexualities as well as gender, such that sadism or masochism, in their dominant and/ or subordinate forms, can operate between gay partners, trans- sexuals, bisexuals, and heterosexuals. All that is required is to be human. But this first connection between Fromm, nonessentialism, and feminism was relatively implicit and in need of being drawn out. A second connection, found in Fromm’s (1956) academically undervalued (perhaps because popularized) The Art of Loving is more obvious and explicit. What of relevance to feminism does Fromm say here about love? Put simply, but profoundly, to love is impossible between two people who are “partial” beings. By contrast, parties who come together as fulfilled beings are likely to find more sustainable joy and happiness, together and apart,

474 LYNN S. CHANCER over time. It is a critique that could be on the same gender-and- sexuality course reading list where one might also find the cri- tique of romance that Simone de Beauvoir (1949) spelled out in literary and quasi-ethnographic detail in The Second Sex. Envision the stuff of young girls’ daydreams, then and now: “ ‘Un jour mon prince viendra . . . .’ Someday, he’ll come along, the man I love— the words of popular songs fill her with dreams of patience and of hope,” Beauvoir recounts (p. 291) about the child who may have been (then and now) influenced by teen romances, or ear- lier by Disney tales of Rapunzel or Cinderella, rescued by hand- some young—and, of course, male lovers. Or imagine girls losing themselves in a country, popular, or hip-hop musical recounting of how, through love, they/we will be completed. It is a romantic form of dependency that Fromm, like Beauvoir, understood to be potentially, psychically crippling—and which overlaps closely with the enculturation of relative powerlessness that traditionally gen- dered notions of “femininity” (and femininities) have inculcated in women from childhood through later ages. Compare Beauvoir’s complaints about such effects of gender on women with Fromm’s (1956) writings, when, in The Art of Lo- ving, he describes the damaging effects of symbiotic love aimed at “fusion” for which the “passive form . . . is masochism” (p. 19). “The masochistic person,” Fromm writes, “escapes from the un- bearable feeling of isolation and separateness by making himself part and parcel of another person who directs him, guides him, protects him; who is his life and his oxygen, as it were” (p. 18). Might not Beauvoir have ignored Fromm’s generic “himself” and substituted how gendered social and cultural influences incline “herself” to experience “feminine” love as, analogously, symbiot- ic? Thus, as Fromm (1956) continues so as to present an alterna- tive: In contrast to symbiotic union, mature love is union under the condition of preserving one’s integrity, one’s individuality. Love is an active power in man [woman]; a power which breaks through the walls which separate man [woman] from his fellow men [women], which unites him [her] with others; love makes him [her] overcome the sense of isolation and separateness, yet it permits him [her] to be himself [herself] to retain his[her] in-

SADOMASOCHISM OR THE ART OF LOVING 475 tegrity. In love the paradox occurs that two beings become one and yet remain two. (p. 19, bracketed words added) While evidently gender critique was not the main aim of The Art of Loving, Fromm’s elegant argument seems strikingly akin not only to Beauvoir’s critique of romance but to later radical femi- nist critiques of patriarchal harm in general. Indeed, as Fromm comprehended, patriarchal inclinations permeated more than so- ciety’s cultural by-products, inside and outside familial walls of living and bedrooms. Sometimes, perhaps too often, these incli- nations were manifested within psychoanalytic offices, too. Here, feminists of diverse persuasions from liberal/radical, to social- ist, to global, and to poststructural would be likely to collectively applaud Fromm’s detailed critique of Freud’s (1905) therapeutic case study “Fragment of an Analysis of a Case of Hysteria.” Accord- ing to Fromm (1956), Dora’s analysis at the hands of Freud should be seen not as a “case study in hysteria” so much as a manifesta- tion of patriarchal dynamics working unconsciously (and perhaps countertransferentially) in Freud, too, within a crippling situation capable of divesting a young woman like Dora of her spunk were it not for the fighting spirit Fromm (not Freud) was able to intuit about her. Here, Fromm emerges as strikingly anti-patriarchal— though he never became particularly known as a feminist-social theorist—simultaneously maintaining his belief in unconscious and psychoanalytically attuned processes while comprehending Dora’s quite feminist-seeming rebellion. This was hardly Freud at his best, of course, as Fromm was willing to state. Proto-feminist, too, is the insight that Dora’s active exit from the analysis was a movement toward liberation; her rejection of the therapy was likely the only way she could emerge as an equal in the experience of love that analysis, ideally, ought itself to prefigure. Finally, a third idea that points to Fromm’s value for feminists is his just-noted offering of a positive rather than exclusively negative critique. In contrast to contemporary social movements (arguably including, sometimes, feminism), which often are bet- ter at protesting “against” injustices rather than presenting prag- matic alternatives, Fromm tried valiantly to offer potentially at- tainable solutions for everyday living. He was committed to sug- gesting positive visions of how human interactions might, much more ideally, look, both within interpersonal relationships and

476 LYNN S. CHANCER as translated into social and political beliefs and values. Again, Fromm’s (1956) Art of Loving provides great assistance even in its simplicity: It sketches, in theory, what is, in practice, a defensible and sustainable picture of relationships far less sexist than what has frequently characterized the patriarchal “norm.” Specifically, love, as portrayed by Fromm, refers to interdependency: One is at once autonomous of and connected with others. Indeed, Fromm’s depiction is extremely close to and compatible with Benjamin’s (1988) advocacy in The Bonds of Love of relationships founded on “mutual recognition.” But what is Benjamin’s notion of mutual recognition, and how does her objects relations–based, psychoanalytically oriented feminism accord with Fromm’s recommendations? Analogously with Fromm, Benjamin’s psychoanalytic feminism differentiates mutual recognition from master/slave or sadomasochistic dy- namics wherein one person takes away the freedom of another in order to (supposedly) ground himself (or herself) as more se- cure. However, the philosophical underpinning of mutual rec- ognition—consonant with Fromm’s ideas—is that in order to be fulfilled, one needs both a satisfying relationship with others and with oneself. In contrast to Fromm, however, Benjamin’s analysis of mutual recognition itself recognizes the hefty role of sexism in skewing and preventing mutual recognition from occurring more regularly and easily. By comparison, throughout his pub- lished oeuvre, Fromm does not accord gender—nor, for that mat- ter, race—the same level of comprehensive analytic consideration as he accorded psychosocial and problematic character structures resulting from capitalist class relations. Nonetheless, it is possible to integrate Fromm’s and Benjamin’s work, just as the fascinating analysis that Eva Illouz (2012) developed in Why Love Hurts: A Sociological Explanation can help to update Fromm’s notions about stubbornly sexist inequities that women (in contrast to men) still often experience when it comes to their contemporary opportu- nities (or not) for experiencing mutually recognizing love. To review, then: In Fromm, one finds ideas that resonate with feminist concerns about the nondeterminist and socially con- structed character of dominance/subordination interactions as these take gendered shapes; the problems of marriage, romance, or any kind of personal/sexual relationships, when based on de- pendent rather than interdependent psychosocial realities; and vi-

SADOMASOCHISM OR THE ART OF LOVING 477 sions, beautifully laid out in The Art of Loving and The Sane Society, of how alternative interpersonal and political connections could look. Why then, in turning to the antithesis of these theses, has Fromm been relatively forgotten—that is, not looked back upon warmly and frequently by present-day feminists? FROMM AND GENDER ESSENTIALISM? EXPLORING A SEEMING CONTRADICTION One reason Fromm is not usually associated with feminist thought stems from the rather cursory observation that, in many of his writings, Fromm refers to “man” when writing generically about the human condition—as the very title of Man for Himself (1947) suggests. This is something that registered for me long ago when I first read Fromm, though an observation I quickly put aside, given the strength and clarity of his ideas overall. On the other hand, in the present context, the usage is notable insofar as it af- fects readers quietly, subliminally. Of course Fromm himself was a product of his time, and the move away from using “man” only became more common when he was in his sixties and seventies, not unlike how the word “Negro” was eventually disavowed and replaced by “Black” in the same period. On the other hand, one wonders whether Fromm ought to have known better since refer- ences to “man” were less starkly noticeable in the work of other Frankfurt School theorists, or in the writing of Sartre or Mills. Fromm was close to eighty when he died in 1980. By then, he might have become familiar with early feminist classics like The Second Sex, possibly even with later feminist texts by Betty Friedan (1963), Kate Millett (2016), and Shulamith Firestone (2003), all published from the late 1960s and through the 1970s. What might have happened? One possibility is that Fromm was unlikely to change his long- accustomed habit of employing the species-oriented “man,” espe- cially if he did not have feminist theorists close by to object. In his thirties and forties, he would have been familiar with proto- feminist thinkers like Karen Horney and Margaret Mead, but in his fifties, he was living in Mexico, far from the American femi- nist upsurge of the 1960s and 1970s. Fromm was distant from the many feminist theorists, from Beauvoir through Firestone, who

478 LYNN S. CHANCER eschewed psychoanalytic perspectives as incompatible with their convictions about the socially constructed character of gender. An exception was Juliet Mitchell (2000) and her book Psychoanaly- sis and Feminism, although she increasingly drew on Lacan, a per- spective not close to Fromm’s own theoretical orientation. Thus, Fromm was never sufficiently motivated to change the arguably sexist character of this recurring linguistic habit. Less easy to grasp is why and how Fromm—despite his con- structionist leanings—came to refer with conviction to biologically based beliefs in “feminine nature.” How can this more theoreti- cally substantive and seemingly curious disparity be explained? In Love, Sexality and Matriarchy: About Gender, Fromm (1997) refers to the anthropological ideas of Johann Bachofen, writing approv- ingly of the latter’s discovery of mother right (p. 4). As Fromm also mentions, Bachofen’s and Lewis Morgan’s anthropological- ly based ideas—that is, that matriarchal societies and principles existed prior to their destruction with the rise of patriarchal so- cieties—were tapped, as well, by Friedrich Engels. According to Bachofen, Friedrich Engels, and later Fromm, patriarchy is rela- tively recent, “and was preceded by a state of culture in which the mother was the head of the family, the ruler in society, and the Great Goddess” (Fromm, 1997, p. 4). Why did this matter so much to Fromm? Unlike Engels’s theo- rization, which links the overthrow of “mother right” to forced monogamy and the beginnings of property, Fromm’s concern is with the rise of cultural and gendered norms that led to psycho- social harms and alienated/alienating character structures within capitalist and patriarchal societies. In Fromm’s (1997) words: As a further consequence, the basic principles of the mother- centered culture are those of freedom and equality, of happi- ness and the unconditional affirmation of life. In contrast to the motherly principles the fatherly principle is that of law, order, reason, hierarchy; the father has his favorite son, the one who is most like him, the most suited to become the heir and successor to his property and worldly functions. Among the father-centered sons, equality has given way to hier- archy, harmony to strike. (pp. 5-6)

SADOMASOCHISM OR THE ART OF LOVING 479 Significant to underscore here is that a determinist stance is there- by suggested, going back to Bachofen; the “essence” of differences between motherly and fatherly love are biologically based insofar as they are linked with women’s role in reproduction (Fromm, 1997, p. 5). Fromm (1997) quotes Bachofen to the effect that “maternity pertains to the physical side of man” (p. 23, emphasis added), adding his own comment that “two traits, therefore, char- acterize the relationship of matriarchal society to nature: passive surrender to nature; and recognition of natural and biological values, as opposed to purely intellectual ones. Like the mother, nature is the center of matriarchal culture; and mankind ever re- mains a helpless child in the face of nature” (p. 23). With this observation, though, a clue emerges to illuminate the ostensible contradiction between Fromm’s typically social-con- structionist (and feminist) writings and the biologism evident in his endeavors to understand how the system that socialist feminist Zillah Eisenstein (1978) dubbed “capitalist patriarchy” evolved. Perhaps, through Bachofen’s allusions to a matriarchal past and the concept of “mother right,” Fromm hoped to reconcile the sa- domasochistic, deeply oppressive inequalities of capitalism—and the pathological deviation of it he witnessed sprouting up in Ger- many via fascism—with his own anti-patriarchal sympathies. The reconciliation for Fromm might have been to posit a “feminine” principle through which the possibilities of a different society based on love, caring, compassion, and mutually recognizing hu- man beings could be envisioned as more than purely utopian. He made this argument with the support of the anthropological documentation that Bachofen and Morgan proffered, evidence and a perspective called into question by contemporary anthro- pologists. By way of evidence for this interpretation, note how Fromm (1997) disagrees, in Love, Sexuality, and Matriarchy, with previous arguments for women’s equality in bourgeois society based on presuming men and women to be (biologically) equal. Making a case resonant of later critiques by radical and socialist feminists of liberal feminists who wanted only formal equality with men, Fromm writes, “The theory that woman and man were identical formed the basis for demanding her political equality. But wheth- er it was expressed or only implied, woman’s equality meant that she, in her very essence, was the same as man in bourgeois society

480 LYNN S. CHANCER . . . .The ‘human’ emancipation of woman really meant her eman- cipation to become a bourgeois male” (Fromm, 1997, p. 26). Does any of this justify Fromm’s essentialism? Not particularly. But it may help to explain this peculiar-seeming biologism by pro- viding insight into why Fromm may have thought himself pro- gressive—and even consistently feminist (if socialist/radical, not liberal feminist!)—when excavating an allegedly matriarchal his- tory to ground imaginings of a humanist future. Even more than this, Fromm may also have felt attracted to biologically tinged notions of unconditional love vis-à-vis his willingness to criticize, indeed to revise, Freudian ideas. Thus, along with, and as influ- enced by Karen Horney, Fromm believed that orthodox Freudian psychoanalytic ideas paid inadequate attention to the significance of motherly love and nurturance in the process of an individual’s development of her or his capacities for empathy and compas- sion. Instead, conventional Freudian psychoanalytic approaches preferred to focus on the alleged centrality of the oedipal and cas- tration complexes, in which patriarchal rather than matriarchal authority in the family was emphasized and reinforced in thera- pists’ minds and practices. The most salient point among these anthropological and psychoanalytic explanations is that both may have appealed to Fromm precisely because they seemed in rather than out of sync with his own feminist and matriarchal sympa- thies. Indeed, as Funk (1956) suggests in the Afterword to one edition of The Art of Loving, maternal love may have been highly resonant in Fromm’s own childhood (p. 12), lending theories of mothering’s centrality even more credence to him. Still, looking back, surely the anthropological effort seems the- oretically futile insofar as projections of origin are not necessary to motivate and effectuate human liberation from sexism and oth- er discriminations. For example, in The Protestant Ethic and the Spi- rit of Capitalism, Max Weber (2013) postulated the origins of our contemporary iron cage of ongoing work, and seemingly endless and driven materialistic accumulation, in early Calvinism and its relationship to emerging capitalism. We no longer recall, Weber observed, why/when/where our own workaholic habits originat- ed. This matters, of course, at one intellectual level; at another, it does not. For wherever and however the “Protestant ethic” origi- nated, an unavoidably pragmatic challenge remains to overcome the recent past and sometimes painful present; in this way, there

SADOMASOCHISM OR THE ART OF LOVING 481 seems little choice but to project from present to future, endeav- oring to criticize and transform psyche and society, regardless of the “original” source of our contemporary discontents. Consequently, perhaps—except at the level of intellectual un- derstanding—Fromm did not need to theorize matriarchal and maternal roots, thereby veering into essentialist territory, in order to comprehend the strength of gender differences that empirical- ly separate men and women, in which the former often becomes/ became more “aggressive” and the latter often becomes/became more “nurturing.” Alternatively, Fromm could have stayed con- sistent with his admirable social constructionist leanings by at- tributing divergent characteristics in men and women not to biol- ogy—that is, women’s “maternal” role in reproduction—but to the deeply sociological enculturation that bequeaths and reproduces gendered patterns from generation to generation or country to country. Clearly, gender socialization differs not only according to class/national background but along racial, sexual, and other intersectioned divergent lines, while still creating clusters of be- haviors and practices across race and class through broad person- ality patterns of “masculinity” (and masculinities) and “feminin- ity” (and femininities). From this, persistent patterns of gender- divided “habituses” can be derived, thereby rendering biological explanations superfluous. Moreover, it is impossible to know what is biological or culturally caused as long as the two are overdeter- mined: Social determinants of gender discrimination would have to wither away entirely to know, for sure, what was or was not bio- logically caused. Nothing of the kind though—that is, elimination of gender’s social concomitants—has yet happened in Fromm’s time or our own. Thus (socially) gendered patterns and the problems of domi- nance/subordination thereby inculcated are more than adequate- ly explanatory—without resorting to theories of origins—to spur social movement protests and theoretical critiques of precisely the kind that have actually marked feminism’s international de- velopment during and beyond Fromm’s lifetime. Where feminists still, arguably, need Fromm is that the psychological/psychoan- alytic part of psychosocially caused gendered effects have been relatively less explored or expanded upon by movements from the second wave of feminism until now. Obviously, as Fromm under-

482 LYNN S. CHANCER stood even better than Freud, given the former’s far more exten- sive critiques of patriarchy and sexism, gendered patterns cause terrible harm to both men and women. These are at once “objec- tive” and “subjective,” social and psychological, acting through de- fense mechanisms, inequitable and authoritarian (gender-skewed) dynamics, and the sexual and psychic guilt and anger these pat- terns impose, sometimes consciously and sometimes not. For this reason, in concluding, I turn at last to whether and how Fromm’s ideas can be rediscovered and reformulated in the present con- text of both rising political authoritarianism and persistent sexist subordinations. How can Fromm’s ideas regarding feminism be reconciled post facto? CONCLUSION: WHY DO FROMM AND FEMINISM MATTER? Perhaps the greatest contribution of Fromm’s thought for con- temporary feminism is its demonstration of theoretical compat- ibility between sociological and psychoanalytic ideas. From the 1960s on, notwithstanding Juliet Mitchell’s (2000) defense in Psy- choanalysis and Feminism, feminists had good reason to be suspi- cious of sexist proclivities and biologically determinist leanings of Freudian theory. Were Fromm’s work better known and more embraced by feminists, an interesting exception could have sur- faced (and still can) to fortify growing and needed interest in the connections of gender, sexuality, and psychoanalysis. Moreover, as emerges so clearly in his critique of Freud’s analysis of Dora, Fromm understood well that the therapeutic process itself could be patriarchal and sexist; depending on the practitioner’s belief and orientations, it could liberate or hinder women’s (and men’s) psychological, social, and sexual development. Then, too, as Funk has underscored, Fromm saw human beings as inherently social; anxiety caused by fear of aloneness, for Fromm, was indeed a “psychosocial” correlate of what Emile Durkheim intended in his use of the term “anomie.” Reflecting the influence of Horney, Fromm’s concerns about anxiety and relatedness led him to an- ticipate aspects of object relations theory later developed in the simultaneously sociological and feminist work not only of Jessica Benjamin but of feminist sociologist and psychoanalyst Nancy Chodorow.

SADOMASOCHISM OR THE ART OF LOVING 483 Can the biological essentialism that appears in some, though by no means all, of Fromm’s writings on gender and sexuality be overlooked? Indeed, should it be? The critique of biologism of- fered here may be partly corrective. But I also wonder if Fromm might have been interested, along with at least some current femi- nists and sociologists, in questioning whether social construction- ist perspectives themselves have limits (or not). Is there anything that defies social constructionist interpretation, whether fear of death, or simply physical differences between people? By now, Fromm’s essentialist view of maternalism seems obso- lescent. It is obvious that men, as well as women, parent and co- parent, sometimes as single parents, in different types of couples, or in group settings from kibbutzim through other forms of com- munal living. Even more importantly, and just as obviously, nur- turance can be (or may not be) provided to infants, regardless of gender, so that empathetic and compassionate ways of relating to oneself and others are able to result. Indeed, what matters most is not gender but the presence or absence of compassion, love, and respect in parent–children as well as adult–adult relationships. Still, one wonders whether the biological and psychological dif- ferences between people were derived from extreme social con- structionism, rendered as if incapable of being broached. With- out resorting to gender essentialism, are there realms of biologi- cal differences that can be referred to without judgment, but with detachment? Or have the extremes of constructionism rendered biology a topic that cannot be discussed without controversy, even as a dimension of life (and death), and without being reduced to the social? While this was not what Fromm had in mind, sociolo- gists and feminists may find that his work invites complexity and multidimensionality to be debated and explored, without, one hopes, fears of sadomasochistic repercussion even within intellec- tual realms. Rather, the spirit of Fromm invites mutual recogni- tion, even theoretically, and as such exists in a relationship both connected to and separate from the feminist perspectives with which his own work and life resonated.
